Tetrarch
TET-rark
noun
From the Greek tetrarchēs, from tetra (“four”) and archē (“rule, dominion”); properly the ruler of a fourth part of a region, and by Roman usage a petty prince under the emperor, lower in dignity than a king. The KJV margin glosses it “governor over four provinces.”

Biblical Definition

A tetrarch is the ruler of a fourth part — a princeling set over a portion of a divided kingdom, holding his little authority at the pleasure of Rome. When Herod the Great died, his realm was parcelled out, and the New Testament’s tetrarchs are the sons and successors who governed the fragments. Luke, writing as an historian and not a fabulist, anchors the coming of the word of God to John in the exact machinery of that government: “in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea… and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene” (Luk 3:1). The gospel did not fall out of the sky into a myth; it entered a dated world of named rulers whose reigns can be counted. Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, is the man the word haunts. He shut John in prison and took his head; and when the fame of Jesus reached him, “he was perplexed” (Luk 9:7), and “said unto his servants, This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead” (Mat 14:1-2). A guilty conscience is a poor counsellor, and the tetrarch who silenced the preacher could not silence the sermon. Yet grace ran through that very household: among the prophets and teachers at Antioch was “Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch” (Act 13:1). The foster-brother was saved; the tetrarch perished. Election, not proximity, makes the difference.

Webster 1828 Definition

A ruler of a fourth part of a province or kingdom; a petty prince under Rome, lower in dignity than a king.

TETRARCH, a Roman governor of the fourth part of a province or kingdom.

From the Greek tetra, “four,” and archē, “rule.”

The KJV margin: “governor over four provinces” (Mat 14:1).

Herod Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee, Philip of Ituraea, Lysanias of Abilene (Luk 3:1).

The title marks a borrowed authority, held at the pleasure of Caesar.

Key Scripture

Mat 14:1 — "At that time Herod the tetrarch heard of the fame of Jesus,"

Luk 3:1 — "Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene,"

Luk 9:7 — "Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead;"

Act 13:1 — "Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul."

Modern Corruption

No postmodern redefinition presses on the word; it recovers that the gospel entered a dated world of named rulers, and that nearness to Christ is not grace.

expand to see more

The title itself preaches a sermon on borrowed authority. A tetrarch is not a king; he is a fourth of one, a man ruling a fragment by the sufferance of a greater throne, and every honour he has is lent. Herod Antipas played the prince, silenced the preacher who reproved him, and took John’s head to keep an oath sworn at a birthday feast — and could not keep his own conscience. When the fame of Jesus came to him he was perplexed, and feared that the Baptist was risen. The man who can command a headsman cannot command his own heart at midnight. All earthly rule is tetrarchy: a portion, held briefly, under the King of kings, to whom the account is owed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, Luke’s dating: he sets the word of God to John in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with Pilate governing and three tetrarchs named to their districts. The canonical narrative is authoritative history, and the coins and inscriptions that name these same men are corroboration, not permission to believe. Second, the household of Herod. Manaen was brought up with the tetrarch and stood at Antioch a prophet of the church; Herod heard John gladly for a season and died an apostate. Two men reared under one roof, one taken and one left. Nearness to the preacher, the palace, or even the pulpit saves no man; the effectual call of God does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the ruler of a fourth part — a petty prince beneath a king.

expand to see more

Tetrarch — Greek tetrarchēs, from tetra + archē.

It denotes the ruler of a fourth part of a divided realm.

Herod the Great’s kingdom was parcelled out among such rulers.

The KJV margin glosses it “governor over four provinces.”

Luke names three tetrarchs to date the coming of the word to John (Luk 3:1).

Usage

"A tetrarch rules a fourth part — all earthly authority is borrowed and briefly held."

"Luke dates the gospel by living tetrarchs: this history happened, in a year men could count."

"Manaen was reared with the tetrarch and preached at Antioch; Herod heard John and perished."
